data.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
data.summary:
Input: A string s and an integer k.
Output: The length of the longest substring containing the same letter you can get after performing at most k character replacements.
Rules: You may choose any character of the string and change it to any other uppercase English character at most k times.
constraints: s consists of only uppercase English letters.

data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    alphabet = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
    s = "".join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(max(1, n)))
    k = rng.randint(0, len(s))
    return [s, k]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    s = "A" * max(1, n)
    k = 0
    return [s, k]

data.key_insight: A window is valid if its length minus the frequency of its most frequent character is less than or equal to k. As we expand the window, we only need to track the maximum frequency seen so far across any valid window.

steps.title: Initialize window pointers and frequency map
steps.detail: Set both left and right pointers to the beginning of the string. Use a dictionary or array to count the frequency of each character in the current window.

steps.title: Expand the right pointer
steps.detail: Iterate through the string with the right pointer, adding each character to the frequency map and updating the maximum frequency of any single character in the window so far.

steps.title: Check window validity and shrink if necessary
steps.detail: If the current window size minus the maximum frequency exceeds k, the window is invalid. Increment the left pointer to shrink the window from the left and update the frequency count.

steps.title: Record the maximum length
steps.detail: The size of the valid window (right - left + 1) is a potential answer. Update the global maximum length at each step.

data.pattern_summary: Sliding window maintains a dynamic range (sub-array or substring) and updates its boundaries incrementally rather than rebuilding from scratch, usually yielding optimal linear time for subarray problems.

pattern_options.name: Sliding Window
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We are looking for the longest substring that satisfies a condition, which can be efficiently tracked by expanding and contracting a window.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While substrings are involved, the problem lacks overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure properties that require a DP table.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A purely greedy choice at each step does not easily account for future replacements or window adjustments without backtracking.

pattern_options.name: Backtracking
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Generating combinations of replacements would be far too slow given the constraint that string lengths can reach 10^5.

signals.hint: Contiguous segments of a sequence often point to sliding window or two-pointer techniques.
A condition threshold that restricts how much a window can expand before needing to shrink.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach checks every possible substring of the string, counts the frequencies of each character inside that substring, and verifies if the number of characters that need to be changed is less than or equal to k.
data.brute_force_why: There are O(n^2) substrings, and for each substring, we iterate through its characters which takes up to O(n) time, resulting in cubic time complexity.
data.bottleneck: Rebuilding and rescanning substrings from scratch for every possible start and end index causes immense redundant work.
bottleneck_hints: Notice how many times the same characters are counted repeatedly across overlapping substrings.
When the end pointer moves forward, do we really need to recount the entire substring from the start pointer?
Think about how you can reuse the frequency counts from the previous window instead of throwing them away.

data.overview: This algorithm uses a sliding window to find the longest substring with the same letter after at most k replacements. It expands the right side and shrinks the left side whenever the number of characters to replace exceeds k.
data.intuition: Imagine stretching a rubber band over a sequence of letters. You can tolerate a few mismatched characters inside the band as long as their count doesn't exceed k.

pitfalls: Forgetting to decrement the frequency of the character at the left pointer when shrinking the window.
Trying to recalculate max_freq from scratch every time the window shrinks, which slows down the algorithm.
Confusing window length minus max_freq with the actual number of allowed replacements k.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: Instead of checking every possible substring from scratch, we maintain a sliding window and expand it as far as possible. When our window becomes invalid because replacements exceed k, we simply shift the left pointer rather than shrinking it to zero. This keeps the window size at its historical maximum or larger, ensuring we only do linear work.

derivation.note: The right pointer iterates through the string of length n exactly once.
Updating character frequency in the hash map takes constant time.
The left pointer only moves forward and never steps backward across the entire run.

data.time_summary: Lines 8 through 17 execute inside a loop controlled by the right pointer, which runs n times. Operations inside the loop take O(1) time. Although the left pointer also moves, it never backtracks, meaning it traverses the string at most once. The total operations scale linearly with n, matching the observed n^1.04 wall-clock growth and yielding O(n) time.
data.space_summary: The hash map char_count stores character frequencies. Because the input consists only of uppercase English letters, the map holds at most 26 keys at any time. This uses O(1) constant auxiliary space.
data.takeaway: When looking for the longest valid substring, use a sliding window that expands on valid states and slides (rather than shrinks completely) on invalid states.
mistakes: Shrinking the left pointer multiple times in a while loop instead of moving it just once per invalid check, which breaks the O(n) guarantee.
Recalculating max_freq from scratch whenever the left pointer moves, instead of maintaining the historical maximum.
Forgetting that max_length does not need to shrink when an invalid window is found because we only care about finding a strictly larger maximum length.
